title: Bronchiolitis and croup
blurb: Tell bronchiolitis from croup, apply NICE NG9 thresholds for oxygen, feeding support and discharge, and give dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for croup.
question: Harper, 3 months, born at term with no underlying conditions, is admitted with bronchiolitis. Her SpO2 has been 91% in air for an hour. Does she need supplemental oxygen?

teach.body: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower respiratory tract infection of babies and young children under 2, most often in the first year, causing inflammation of the small airways. Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a viral infection causing swelling around the larynx and trachea, giving a barking cough and stridor. Plain English: bronchiolitis is a chesty baby who struggles to feed; croup is a toddler with a seal-like bark and noisy breathing in. Treatment is very different.
teach.cite: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis (updated 2021); NICE CKS Croup

rows.label: Course
values: Worst days 3–5; cough may last 3 weeks
Often worse at night; better within 48 h

teach.caption: Both usually start with a runny nose and cold-like symptoms for a few days.

head: Group
Give oxygen if SpO2 persistently
Discharge if SpO2 in air for 4 h
teach.caption: The 4 hours must include a period of sleep. Also check the child is clinically stable and taking adequate oral fluids.

steps.label: 999 now
steps.sub: Apnoea, looks seriously unwell, grunting, marked recession, RR over 70, central cyanosis

steps.label: Consider referral
steps.sub: RR over 60, intake 50–75% of usual, dehydration, SpO2 under 92%

steps.label: Home
steps.sub: Safety-netting: red flags, feeding, who to call

teach.caption: Babies under 6 weeks may present with apnoea alone, without other signs.

teach.body: NG9 says do not use antibiotics, hypertonic saline, nebulised adrenaline, salbutamol, montelukast, ipratropium or steroids. Care is oxygen at the thresholds above, help with feeding (nasogastric or orogastric fluids if the baby cannot take enough by mouth), and suction only when secretions cause distress or feeding difficulty, or with apnoea. Do not routinely do blood tests, chest X-ray or blood gases. Consider CPAP for impending respiratory failure.

items.label: nebulised budesonide if oral not tolerated
IM dexamethasone: alternative if oral not tolerated
nebulised adrenaline with oxygen, senior help

teach.caption: Keep the child calm and upright on a parent's lap. Do not examine the throat. Do not use steam.

teach.text: Nebulised adrenaline belongs to severe croup, not bronchiolitis. NG9 lists nebulised adrenaline, salbutamol and steroids among treatments NOT to use in bronchiolitis, whereas a single dose of dexamethasone is given to every child with croup.

teach.body: Theo has a barking cough. Now he has stridor at rest, moderate sternal recession and is agitated. Nurse Joy keeps him on his mother's lap, avoids upsetting procedures and does not look in his throat. She escalates to the registrar for severe croup. Oxygen and nebulised adrenaline are given, with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, and she watches closely as the adrenaline effect can wear off.

items: Sit the child upright and keep them calm; crying worsens symptoms.
Offer plenty of fluids and check on them regularly, including at night.
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever or discomfort.
Call 999 if struggling to breathe, blue or grey, drowsy, drooling or cannot be calmed.
Bronchiolitis: under 2, peak 3–6 months; worst days 3–5; supportive care only.
Oxygen if SpO2 persistently under 90% (6 weeks+) or under 92% (under 6 weeks or underlying condition).
Discharge: stable, feeding, SpO2 above threshold in air for 4 h including sleep.
999: apnoea, grunting, marked recession, RR over 70, central cyanosis.
Croup: single oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; nebulised adrenaline if severe; no throat exam.

summary: You can now distinguish bronchiolitis from croup and apply NG9 oxygen, feeding, referral and discharge rules. You can also give the correct croup treatment and keep a child with stridor calm and safe.

A.q: Harper, 3 months, born at term with no underlying conditions, has bronchiolitis. Her SpO2 has been 91% in air for an hour. Does she need oxygen?
options: Yes, as she is under 6 months
Yes, as her SpO2 is below 92% in air
Yes, as she is under 1 year
No, as her SpO2 is 90% or above
A.why: NG9: for children aged 6 weeks and over without underlying conditions, give oxygen if SpO2 is persistently under 90%. At 91% she does not need it.

whyNot.0: The age cut-off for the higher threshold is 6 weeks, not 6 months.
whyNot.1: The 92% threshold applies under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions.
whyNot.2: Being under 1 year does not change the 90% threshold for her.

A.q: Ruby, 2, wakes at night with a barking cough and noisy breathing in. At rest she is settled with no stridor. What treatment is recommended?
A.why: CKS: a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is recommended for croup of all severities.

whyNot.1: Salbutamol treats lower airway narrowing, not croup.
whyNot.2: Steam is not recommended for croup.
whyNot.3: Croup is viral; antibiotics are not indicated.

A.q: Which treatment does NICE NG9 recommend NOT using for bronchiolitis?
options: Nasogastric feeds if intake is poor
A.why: NG9 rec 1.4.3: do not use salbutamol (or antibiotics, hypertonic saline, nebulised adrenaline, montelukast, ipratropium or steroids) in bronchiolitis.

whyNot.0: NG or OG fluids are recommended if the baby cannot take enough orally.
whyNot.2: Oxygen is recommended below the NG9 thresholds.
whyNot.3: Suction is considered when secretions cause distress or feeding difficulty.

B.q: Ava, 3 weeks, born at 39 weeks, has a two-day cold. While being observed, she has a pause in breathing. What should happen?
B.why: Apnoea (observed or reported) is an indication for emergency care in NG9, and babies under 6 weeks may present with apnoea alone.

whyNot.0: Waiting 4 hours after an apnoea is unsafe.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol is not used in bronchiolitis and does not treat apnoea.
whyNot.2: Apnoea requires emergency care, not discharge.

B.q: Jacob, 5 months, has bronchiolitis. He is tiring with feeds and taking about half his usual milk. His SpO2 is 93% in air. What support is most appropriate?
B.why: NG9: give fluids by nasogastric or orogastric tube if the baby cannot take enough fluid by mouth.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics are not used in bronchiolitis.
whyNot.1: Steroids are not used in bronchiolitis.
whyNot.3: Chest physiotherapy is not done without relevant comorbidities.

B.q: Maisie, 7 months, has bronchiolitis. For the last 4 hours, including a sleep, her SpO2 has stayed at 93–95% in air. She is feeding well and stable. What should the nurse expect?
B.why: NG9 rec 1.5.1: discharge when clinically stable, taking adequate oral fluids and SpO2 over 90% in air for 4 hours including sleep (6 weeks and over).

whyNot.1: She already meets the discharge criteria.
whyNot.2: Routine chest X-ray is not recommended.
whyNot.3: Routine blood gas testing is not recommended.

C.q: Leon, 9 months, has bronchiolitis on day 4. His respiratory rate rises to 74 and he is grunting with marked recession. What should the nurse do?
C.why: Grunting, marked recession and RR over 70 are severe distress signs that need emergency escalation; CPAP may be needed for impending respiratory failure.

whyNot.1: Hypertonic saline is not used in bronchiolitis.
whyNot.2: Increasing feeds risks aspiration in a child in severe distress.
whyNot.3: Waiting 2 hours delays care for a child in severe distress.

C.q: Theo, 18 months, has croup with stridor at rest, moderate recession and agitation. While waiting for the doctor, what should the nurse do?
options: Look in his throat with a pen torch
Keep him calm on his mother's lap
C.why: Keep a child with stridor calm and upright, ideally with a parent. Distress worsens airway obstruction.

whyNot.0: Examining the throat can precipitate complete obstruction.
whyNot.1: Lying flat may worsen breathing; upright is better.
whyNot.2: Upsetting procedures can worsen stridor and should wait.

C.q: Mila, 2, weighs 12 kg and has croup. Oral dexamethasone is prescribed. What dose is correct?
C.why: 0.15 mg/kg x 12 kg = 1.8 mg as a single oral dose.

whyNot.0: 7.2 mg is 0.6 mg/kg, the IM alternative dose.

reteach.title: Bark or wheeze?
reteach.question: How do the sound, age and treatment help you tell croup from bronchiolitis?

blocks.body: A seal-like bark with noisy breathing in (stridor) points to swelling high in the airway: croup. Treat with one dose of oral dexamethasone. Wheeze or crackles in a baby who is struggling to feed point to the small airways: bronchiolitis. There is no drug that helps, so care is oxygen, feeding support and watching for red flags.

blocks.text: The oxygen threshold depends on age and health: under 90% for babies 6 weeks and over, under 92% for under 6 weeks or with an underlying condition.

explain.body: Coryzal prodrome 1 to 3 days, then cough with tachypnoea or recession, plus wheeze or crackles. Worst on days 3 to 5. Fever over 39°C or persistent focal crackles suggests pneumonia instead.

test.q: When are bronchiolitis symptoms usually at their worst?
test.why: NG9: symptoms usually peak between days 3 and 5 of the illness.

whyNot.1: Day 1 is usually the coryzal phase.
whyNot.2: By days 10 to 14 most are improving.
whyNot.3: By week 3 the cough has resolved in 90%.

explain.body: Oxygen if SpO2 persistently under 90% (6 weeks+) or under 92% (under 6 weeks or underlying conditions). Discharge when stable, feeding and above those levels in air for 4 hours including sleep.

test.q: Noor, 4 weeks old, has bronchiolitis. At what persistent SpO2 should oxygen be given?
test.why: Under 6 weeks the threshold is persistently under 92%.

whyNot.1: 90% applies to babies aged 6 weeks and over without underlying conditions.

explain.body: No antibiotics, hypertonic saline, nebulised adrenaline, salbutamol, montelukast, ipratropium or steroids in bronchiolitis. No routine bloods, chest X-ray, blood gas or suction.

test.q: A parent asks for steroids for her baby with bronchiolitis. What is the nurse's best answer?
options: Steroids are given if wheeze is present
Inhaled steroids can be used instead
test.why: NG9 rec 1.4.3: systemic or inhaled corticosteroids are not used for bronchiolitis.

whyNot.0: Wheeze in bronchiolitis does not respond to steroids.
whyNot.1: Inhaled steroids are also listed as not to be used.
whyNot.2: Illness duration does not change the recommendation.

explain.body: Barking cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor, often worse at night; usually better within 48 hours. Single oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; nebulised budesonide 2 mg or IM dexamethasone if oral not tolerated; nebulised adrenaline for severe.

test.q: A child with croup is vomiting and cannot keep oral medicine down. What alternative can be used?
test.why: CKS: if oral dexamethasone is not tolerated, nebulised budesonide 2 mg (or IM dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg) can be used.

whyNot.1: Oral prednisolone is also oral and will not be tolerated.
whyNot.3: Croup is viral; antibiotics are not indicated.
